In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The Surah of al-Ghashiyah (The Overwhelming): its purpose

It explains what is at the end of "Sabbih" (Surah 87) concerning the glorification of Allah, exalted is He, above vanity, by affirming the Last Abode, whose beginning is the Ghashiyah (the Overwhelming Event). It mentions what is in it for the righteous and the wretched, and the proof of Allah's power over it. The most indicative of what is in it for this purpose is the Ghashiyah itself. We seek refuge in Allah from a heart that is overwhelmed and an insight that is overwhelmed, lest the Ghashiyah come upon us, arising from evil deeds.

"In the name of Allah" (Bismillah), to whom belongs complete majesty and dazzling wisdom. "The Most Gracious" (al-Rahman), to whom belongs the highest overflowing bounty and manifest blessings. "The Most Merciful" (al-Rahim), who chose friends and set right the inner dimensions of their blessings, until these became manifest and pure.

* *

When "Sabbih" was concluded with the exhortation to purify souls from the filth of this world, and with encouragement to this by the excellence of the Hereafter at one time and by following the Messengers of firm resolve (ulu al-azm) among the prophets at another, the beginning of this surah was a warning against turning away from that once, and against purifying oneself by other than the way of the Messengers another time. So He, exalted is He, said, reminding of the Hereafter, which the end of the previous surah had urged:

Establishing for the noblest of His creation ﷺ, because that is greater in establishing his following and more firmly moves souls to receive the report with acceptance: "Has there come to you" (hal ataka), that is, has it reached you and befallen you clearly, O greatest of our creation, "the report of the Overwhelming" (hadith al-ghashiyah), that is, the Resurrection, which overwhelms people with its great calamities, terrors and warnings, for overwhelming happens only in what is disliked.

Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When His glorification, exalted is He, above what the wrongdoers imagined had preceded, and the surah continued in what makes clear the holiness of the Creator, majestic is His majesty, above their grave speech, He followed that with mention of the Ghashiyah, after opening the surah in the form of a question, to magnify its matter. So He said to His Prophet ﷺ: "Has there come to you" O Muhammad "the report of the Overwhelming?" which is the Resurrection. [So it is as if] He, glorified and exalted, is saying: On that day they will see their recompense, and their regret will intensify when it will not avail them. Then He described their great trial in His saying: "They have no food except from a thorny plant" (Al-Ghashiyah 88:6), together with what follows it and precedes it. Then He described the state of those who were in the opposite of their state, since that is more increasing in joy and more severe. Then He followed with mention of the signs He set up and how they did not suffice, so He said: "Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?" (Al-Ghashiyah 88:17) and the verses that follow, that is: do they not take warning from all of that and reason from the craftsmanship to the Craftsman? Then He commanded him to remind - end.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 88, verse 2:

When He had magnified its matter by its indeterminacy and generality, He increased the magnitude further by what He mentioned of its conditions in dividing people into the wretched and the happy. He began with the wretched because the context is a warning to those who prefer the worldly life. The detailed division justified beginning with the indefinite noun, so He said: ﴿Faces﴾, meaning very many, existing ﴿on that Day﴾ [meaning] when it envelops people, ﴿humbled﴾, meaning abased and submissive, from shame, disgrace, fear, and regret, which does not benefit at such a time.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 88, verse 3:

﴿Working﴾ means striving in the deeds by which they seek salvation, since there is no salvation once the abode of action has passed. So you see them toiling at what the Zabaniyah (the angels of punishment) impose on them: dragging chains and shackles, and wading through the torrents of fire, and the like. It is as if it is said to one of them: "Discharge the trust," and then his trust is represented to him at the bottom of Hell. So he is made to descend to it, then he carries it on his neck and climbs the mountains of fire until, when he nearly reaches their summit, it falls from him, and he is made to descend to it again, and so on. This is because he used to neglect action in the world. ﴿Toiling﴾ means that they are, in that, in the utmost state of fatigue and exhaustion through labour and striving. This is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, because they did not fear Allah in the world, so they did not act for Him, and they did not weary their bodies in His obedience. Therefore, on that Day, He subjected them to something greater than what they had endured in the world, with harm and no benefit. It is also possible that it refers to those who wore out and exhausted their bodies in the world while being upon other than the religion of Islam, such as the monks of the Christians after the abrogation (of their religion), and the heretical Sufis among the philosophers and their followers. In that case, "faces" (wujuh) is the subject (mubtada') and "on that Day" (yawma'idhin) is its predicate (khabar), meaning: existing on that Day. Then what follows is supplied as an answer to a questioner who asks: "What is their state?" So he is answered with His saying: ﴿humbled﴾, that is, in the world, and so on to the end. This is the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, in the narration of 'Ata' from him.

Since punishment can only be [on] what the one being punished dislikes, this indicates that [it is] on this, and that it is at its most severe when the verb is in the passive form, in the recitation of Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim. So He said: ﴿Is made to burn﴾, meaning that a person causes it to be entered in the easiest and simplest manner, by the command of the One who has the command, by forcing it to be immersed so that it completely encompasses it. The meaning according to the recitation of the majority, with the active form, is: it enters and makes contact, as its people thrust it into it, so that it surrounds it from every side. This indicates the utmost humiliation, because whoever does this to himself can only be in this state. ﴿A fierce, blazing fire﴾, intensely hot, because it acted in ignorance contrary to what its Prophet had set down for it, so it failed in a pillar of the action or a condition of it, due to the heedlessness that dominated it and surrounded it. Therefore no place was left in it where mercy could enter.

Since whoever is in the heat is most in need of something whose inside is cool, he said, building the verb in the passive (and this is the reading of all, following the recitation of Abu 'Amr in the preceding verse): ﴿They will be made to drink﴾, meaning: every one whom the King has permitted in that will be given to drink, in the easiest and most convenient manner ﴿from a boiling spring﴾, meaning one that has reached its utmost in heat, so that it has been cooked to the utmost degree of cooking. So when they bring it near them, the flesh of their faces falls off, and when they drink, it cuts their intestines apart, [in return for] the cups of desire that they drank in this world, with which their delight in them cut the hearts of the friends of God.

When he had mentioned what they are given to drink, with knowledge of it, that it neither nourishes nor quenches thirst from thirst, he followed it with what they are given to eat, and said, confining it to them: ﴿They have no food﴾, i.e., these people who wasted their souls in worship that God had not permitted, ﴿except from ḍarīʿ﴾, i.e., dried-up shabraq (a thorny plant that camels graze while it is moist, but when it dries out they avoid it, and it is poisonous). [And] al-Qamus (the dictionary) said: "al-ḍarīʿ, like amīr: shabraq, or its dryness, or the plant when it is moist is called shabraq, and when it is dry it is called ḍarīʿ; no beast comes near it because of its foulness; or it is something in Hell more bitter than aloes, more foul-smelling than carrion, and hotter than fire; and it is a foul-smelling plant that the sea casts up." Al-Harawi in al-Gharibayn and ʿAbd al-Haqq in al-Wāʿī said: "al-ḍarīʿ is the shabraq, which is a well-known thorny plant in the Hijaz; it is called shabraq while it is moist, and when it dries it is ḍarīʿ." Al-Qazzaz said in his Diwan: "al-ḍarīʿ is the dryness of some trees." It was also said: "It is specifically the dryness of the shabraq." It was said: "It is a green plant that the sea casts up, and it is foul-smelling."

Abu Hanifa (p-6), may God have mercy on him, said: "It is a pasture on which the grazing animal does not build up fat or meat, and if it does not leave it for another, its condition becomes bad." Ibn al-Athir said in al-Nihayah: "al-ḍarīʿ is a plant in the Hijaz with large thorns." And he said: "al-shabraq is a Hijazi plant that is eaten and has thorns, and when it dries it is called al-ḍarīʿ." And this is a garment that is mushbaraq, which is one that has been spoiled, and in whose weave there is weakness. And shabraqtu al-thawb also means: you burned it. Al-Qamus said: "al-shabraq, like zibrij: the moist ḍarīʿ, its singular is with the ending bahāʾ." Al-Baghawi, may God have mercy on him, said: Mujahid, Qatada and ʿIkrima said: "It is a thorny plant lying flat on the ground, which Quraysh call al-shabraq; when it grows rough, they call it al-ḍarīʿ, and it is the most foul and most repulsive food." This is the narration of al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both. It is not impossible, in the power of God, glorified and exalted be He, that al-ghislīn, when it flows off the bodies of the people of the Fire, takes the form of the shabraq called ḍarīʿ, so their food would be the ghislīn, which is the ḍarīʿ. It is also possible that this is a metaphor for the most wretched kind of living, and not meant to refer to any specific thing; and God knows best. Al-Mulawi said: "It was called ḍarīʿ because a person humbles himself (yataḍarraʿu) when eating it, because of its roughness, bitterness and stench."

When he restricted their food to this, and it was known among the Arabs that *al-ḍarīʿ* (a thorny, bitter plant) might be thought to be a food which, if forced upon someone, would fatten him or satisfy his hunger, and since the *ḍarīʿ* that they eat on the Day of Resurrection is thorns of Fire, as its interpretation was transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), he negated the benefit of food. So he said, describing the *ḍarīʿ*, or the food that is implied after "except" by what is understood from it, by the avoidance of camels, which graze on every growing plant and are the greatest of animals in their eagerness for kinds of thorns, that it is a harm without benefit: ﴿Neither fattens﴾, that is, it does not satisfy and does not strengthen, because fattening is entailed, so its absence entails the absence of fattening.

When he negated what is sought by people of comfort, and began with it because the context requires it, he negated what is sought for mere sufficiency, so he said, exalted is He: ﴿nor does it satisfy﴾, that is, it does not suffice as an initial sufficiency, ﴿from hunger﴾. So it does not preserve health nor prevent emaciation. The purpose of food is one of these two matters. This is because they used to eat the unlawful, upon which their flesh grows, so it corrupts them by its corruption, and their souls grow by it, so it makes them evil by its evil. They also feed on doubtful matters and engage in them at all times, and they engage in the sciences that darken the hearts, such as philosophy, poetry, magic, and the like, which lead to innovations.

This verse is an instance of *al-ihtibāk* (a rhetorical device in which one element is mentioned and its counterpart is omitted, to be understood from the other): the negation of fattening first implies the affirmation of emaciation second, and the negation of satisfying from anguish second implies the negation of being sated first. Whoever takes this as a description of the food has corrupted the meaning, because it would lead to: "They have no food from which fattening and satisfying are negated, but rather they have food which does not negate these."

When he mentioned the enemies and placed them first because of what preceded, he followed them with the friends (awliya'). Beginning a new statement, he said, mentioning what they have in contrast to what was mentioned for the enemies: ﴿Faces that Day﴾, i.e. [since] what was mentioned was the case, ﴿radiant﴾, meaning possessing brightness and joy, upon which blessing, freshness, comfort and ease appear, in opposition to that toiling state. This is because these people wearied themselves in the abode of action, the lower world, and endured asceticism and the hardship of living.

Translation:

[Her] striving: that is, her works for the Hereafter, which are as though there were no striving other than them, especially since she knows that it will save her. [She is] pleased: because of what she saw of its reward, she wishes that all her striving [in this world] had been for that, after that striving which is for the Hereafter had been hateful to her in this world, so that she would not undertake it except with great difficulty.

When he mentioned the striving, He followed it with its reward, so He said: ﴿In a lofty garden﴾, meaning in a high place and an elevated station, with trees and chambers and other things, because they turned their souls away from base things and raised their aspirations (himam) to precious things.

When what has been said of this is not pure, and in it there is what is disliked of speech, He said, exalting it above every evil: ﴿You will not hear﴾, i.e., O you who enter it — according to the reading of the majority (al-jama'ah). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ruways from Ya'qub read it in the passive voice (al-bina' lil-maf'ul), and this is more emphatic in negation: ﴿therein any idle talk﴾, i.e., some idle talk, or a soul that engages in idle talk, or a word possessing idle talk, according to the metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi). Rather, what is heard therein is the remembrance (al-dhikr) of praise (al-tahmid), glorification (al-tamjid), and declaring God free of imperfection (al-tanzih), so that what is seen therein of wonders is borne toward that, with the removal of the worldly desires (al-huzuz) that would carry the hearts toward other than this, from the idle talk of the people of this world, which is incompatible with wisdom, and which they used to dislike.

(p-10) When he described Paradise by the first quality that is considered in it, which is the absence of anything that disturbs, he followed it with what is sought after that, which is the enjoyment of delights. Eating had already been understood from the mention of the word "Paradise," so he mentioned the drink on its own, both because of that and because of what it indicates when it is flowing, along with the increase in Paradise's beauty and the abundance within it of nourishing and delightful plants, fruits, trees, irrigation, and birds. He said, since not every garden we know of has flowing water by itself: ﴿in it﴾, i.e., in Paradise. Since flowing water is suitable to be divided among many places, and he specified his statement, the intended meaning being the genus that includes the many, as a counterpart to the springs of the people of the Fire in the abode of perdition: ﴿a flowing spring﴾, i.e., greatly flowing, very much so, such that it never ceases at all, because of the purity and generosity of its earth and the abundance and goodness of the essence of its water. So it is suitable to cover all its regions, its farthest and nearest parts, even if its expanse is great and its territories and tracts are distant, as we see it flowing from the trunk of a very large tree, watering all its branches, leaves, and fruits. It exceeds that in that its flow is from below upward, drawn by the pull of longing and driven by it, i.e., a driving that the All-Knowing Creator determines. And He who is able to do this, as is witnessed by us, there is no doubt that He is able to make this spring, suitable for the genus even if it is one in person, cover all the facilities of Paradise, [flowing] to its tents, gardens, orchards, reservoirs, and assemblies, and ascending to the high parts of its chambers, however high they may be, divided according to what is beneficial, distributed according to the measure of uses, with utmost precision, along with what is in its interior of humility, which makes tears flow from them, reduces sleep, and increases thirst and hunger.

(p-11) When nothing remained after eating and drinking but reclining, He said, conveying that they are kings: ﴿Therein﴾, repeating the predicate to break off the sentence from the first (i.e., starting a new clause), as an alert to the nobility of the spring, because water is something life cannot exist without. ﴿Thrones﴾, meaning exceeding limit in abundance, the plural of sarir (throne), which is a high seat on which the king sits and is carried to whatever place he desires. It was so named because it gladdens the soul (yasurru al-nafs), and the root as a whole relates to joy, goodness and nobility; for this reason it is applied to kingship, blessing and comfortable living. ﴿Raised high﴾, meaning a great Raiser has raised them [in height], which is the direction of above, so that the one seated upon them may see all his dominion, what he enjoys of it, and what God has willed beyond it; and in measure, not as you know them in this world. Rather, their elevation is a sublime form proportionate to the greatness of the One who raised them, who raised the heaven. Thus the indefiniteness (in "raised") is for magnification, and the name is built in the passive form to indicate that it has, in its own essence, nothing but lowness, while its elevation comes from the compulsion of the One capable of all things. This indicates [that they are] like a heaven without pillars. Al-Baghawi said: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: Its cushions are of gold, adorned with emeralds, pearls and rubies, elevated as long as its people have not come; when one wishes to sit upon them, they lower themselves for him until he sits upon them, then they rise back to their places, end of quote. This is in contrast to what they used to do, humbling themselves and laboring in the hardships of worship upon the dust, so they inherit garments.

(p-12) Since the one at rest needs to repeat drinking, and [needs] that from which he drinks, He said: ﴿And cups﴾, plural of kub, which is a vessel without a handle, so it is suitable for being passed around and for drinking from every direction, ﴿set in place﴾, i.e., full, and they are in such a position that it is easy for them to reach for them.

Since one who is in this state needs supports and abundant cushions, God the Exalted said: ﴿And cushions﴾, meaning supports on which they lean. It is the plural of namruqa, with a fatha or a damma on the first letter, and it is the pillow (wisada). ﴿Arranged in rows﴾, meaning some of them placed next to others, so that they are in the greatest abundance, as if they were the hills piled up upon the carpet of the earth.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 88, verse 16:

﴿And carpets﴾ meaning broad spreads, thick with pile, as if they were meadows, splendid and lush, set apart from the places where they rest. The word is the plural of zarabiyyah (a single carpet), ﴿spread out﴾, meaning laid out scattered in places not intended for leisurely enjoyment, among the sprouting herbs and the intertwined trees, just as He, glory be to Him, spread out the surface of the earth and adorned it with kinds of splendid vegetation, by which they spread out their selves in this world for the Truth and made them soft for it.

When Allah, glorified is He, had finished describing that abode in the manner suited to these short surahs, and they were extremely stubborn in their denial, He rebuked them with a denying interrogation that would keep them from deviating from the sound beliefs. It reminded them of matters that are most evident in themselves, because the revelation of these surahs came at the beginning of the matter, before they had trained themselves in the knowledge (ma'arif) that points to His power to resurrect and to His power over what He mentioned, namely these things that He placed in the gardens for the enjoyment of man. This is because of what is in these matters that He mentioned, of the wonders of His craftsmanship, along with their variety: some of them He made capable of choice in lowering and raising, while others are in a single state, with no ability to depart from it, whether high or low, level or rough. So He said, as a consequence of what had passed concerning the report about the conditions of the two groups in the Hereafter and about His power over what He mentioned: ﴿Do they not look﴾, that is, the deniers of this community, at the power of Allah, glorified and exalted, over the Garden and what He mentioned in it, [and the Fire and what He mentioned in it -] with a look of contemplation (nazar i'tibar).

Since they had a closer association with camels than with other animals, and since the camel is unique among created beings, having no equal, along with its many benefits, as al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said, and since it eats every pasture and is content with the least of things, especially water, and endures thirst for a long time despite its great size, its bulk and its immense strength, it was more indicative of complete power and of action by choice. He said, drawing attention by mentioning it to reflection upon the signs scattered among the animals, which are the most noble of conveyances and the most intricate in their making, after He had pointed to their indication of resurrection in the surah of al-Buruj by mentioning Thamud, after He had explicitly stated it in the surah of ... [the text says "سورة سبحانه"], as its explanation passed in both places, and as will come, Allah willing, in al-Fajr and al-Shams. He explained the expression about it here with what indicates intermingling that inclines and transforms, which suits the meaning of al-Ghashiyah, unlike the expression in Surat al-Nahl, where it is called "al-an'am" (livestock), because that is the surah of blessings. ﴿at the camels﴾. He drew attention to the fact that the wonder of their creation is something that should attract the strong motives of questioning and inquiry about it with the interrogative particle. So He said, using the passive form to indicate that what points to it is contemplation of the mere fact of their creation, which indicates the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah, His great benevolence, His power, His exalted action by choice, and the excellence of His management, in that He created them to haul burdens [to distant lands], and made them great, kneeling for loading, rising with it without a fixed condition, submissive to whoever leads them, long of neck, so that they bear heavy loads. They graze on every plant and endure thirst for ten days or more, so that crossing deserts becomes possible through them. Thus they are the ships of the land, along with their other benefits. Al-Baydawi said: For this reason they were singled out for mention, to show the signs scattered among the animals, which are the most noble of conveyances and the most intricate in their making, [and] because they are the most wondrous thing among the Arabs, end of quote. They are docile for being led, and in their travel they are greatly moved by a beautiful voice. Among their wonders is that they never lie at all, for they do not kneel [out of inability to bear the load -] except when no strength remains in them. There is nothing in them whose dislike is general except the abundance of their groaning. Perhaps for this reason Allah, glorified is He, negated idle talk (laghw) from the Garden. Perhaps it is like the flowing spring and its nearness to its milk, and the raised couches, which it is reported lower themselves until the one who benefits from them can mount them, and then rise with him to the sky in its height, along with what they know of camels kneeling for loading and riding. Then their rising for complete benefit, and the nearness of the placing of the cups by their humps and the cushions by their remaining parts while kneeling. Then He distinguished what the camels indicate of the cups by mountains that cannot be ascended, like the mountain of the barrier, and the cushions by those that can be ascended, and the spreading of the carpets by the cradled earth. Abu Hayyan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: ﴿How﴾ is a question about a state, and the element governing it is ﴿was created﴾. When the verb is suspended from what contains the interrogation, the interrogation does not remain in its literal sense.

And when He, glory be to Him and exalted, mentioned this singular creature, which is the strongest indication of the view that [things operate] by nature, He followed it with the mention of the sky, so that the listener would be reminded of this and would keep far from whoever holds that view. So He said: ﴿And at the sky﴾, that is, the one which is among Our creatures, ﴿how it was raised﴾, that is, its raising came about with the greatest ease from the One who created it, without pillars, given its vastness, greatness, weight and firmness, and what is in it of stars, marvels and wonders. This indicates the complete power, in which none of Him, exalted is He, shares with anyone, whether small or great, in bringing into existence the lofty Paradise and in raising the couches [in it]. For this indicates action by choice, and negates the rule of nature both as a judgment and as a necessity, and this indicates the perfection of His power, exalted is He, over everything.

When al-Biqa'i (may Allah have mercy on him) had mentioned the high among animals, which are associated with humans, and the high among the created beings, he followed it with the highest of the earth, and so Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And at the mountains﴾, meaning the lofty ones, and they are the most solid of the earth, ﴿how they were raised up﴾, meaning: their being raised, by the one who raised them, very high above the rest of the earth, without any cause in them for that, from nature or otherwise, but by the act of a chooser who acts by choice. So they are firmly fixed and do not sway. He placed them in that state, along with the benefits in them, such as flowing waters and diverse trees, which is more wondrous than the placing of cups and decorated cushions. Through them the earth was also held steady and protected from shaking, and the matter of the stars was balanced in determining the night and the day, through the equilibrium of the lands with openness, by raising some of them above others, until the risings and the settings followed a constant order and a firm, unbroken system, by which the times, the seasons, the years, the days and the months are measured, along with other matters. None of this would be theirs except by an all-powerful, capable, choosing Lord who has no partner.

Since lowering cannot occur except by a dominating lowerer, just as raising is likewise, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And at the earth﴾, that is, with its vastness, ﴿how it was spread out﴾, that is, its spreading was accomplished by the One who spread it until it became a couch laid out, upon which one walks with the utmost ease. The capacity to make it thus, along with what it contains of adornment through luxuriant vegetation and other varieties, is an indication of action by choice, and it is not without the power to scatter carpets throughout Paradise, in their diverse forms, shapes, and colors.

When what he mentioned of the wonders of His craftsmanship in the kinds of creatures, both the simple and the compound, the heavenly and the earthly, pointed to the perfection of His power [over everything, which pointed to the perfection of His power -] to the Resurrection, and to everything he mentioned that He does (p-18) in Paradise and Hell, and the urging to reflect on these things was phrased as a denying question, and that implied the absence of reflection, He, glorified is He, said, consequently upon it: ﴿So remind﴾, everyone whose remembrance and benefit from reminding is hoped for, O best of our creation, by what is in their natural dispositions and innate natures of knowledge, the primary knowledge of these things and their like, which indicates the soundness of what We sent down to you, so that it may show them the perfection of the power of the One who sent you, and they will submit to you with the fullest submission, especially in believing in the truth of the Resurrection. Let it not concern you that they do not reflect or take a stand. Perhaps reminding brings the one who is reminded, if he turns to it with a good desire, to know that camels resemble the tranquil, humbled, obedient, and compliant souls, the sky resembles the holy, luminous spirits, the mountains resemble the intellects and the firm, established knowledges, and the earth resembles the body that contains the limbs and the pillars.

Since this surah is Meccan and among the first things revealed, and he was at that time commanded to overlook (the offenses of the unbelievers), he said: ﴿You are only a reminder﴾, that is, not a compelling warrior forcing them to remember and return (p-19). So there is no fault on you if they do not reflect and do not remember, for there is nothing upon you except conveying the message, and for this reason He said

﴿You are not﴾. He alluded to dominance by using the particle of elevation (ʿalā, "over"), saying: ﴿over them﴾, meaning specifically, ﴿a controller﴾, that is, a ruler over them. As for others, ﴿We will soon give you power over them﴾. Al-Kisa'i recited it with the sīn (bi-muṣayṭir → bi-musayṭir), according to the original form.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 88, verse 23:

When He negated for them (the disbelievers) any domination over them (by the Prophet) (تُسَلِّطُ الدُّنْيا?) — and the implied meaning was: "Whoever turns back and believes, then Allah will bestow upon him the greatest bounty" — He said, correcting (their case) in the form of an exception, as a counterpart to them: ﴿Except﴾, meaning "but," ﴿for whoever turns away﴾, meaning he imposes upon his tranquil soul and his original, upright disposition (fitrah) the act of turning away, ﴿and disbelieves﴾, meaning he persists in his disbelief. And he answered the conditional with his words, as a consequence of it:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 88, verse 24:

﴿Then Allah will punish him﴾ with the greatest punishment, which neither the hardest iron nor the strongest mountains can endure. ﴿Allah﴾, that is, the Greatest King, because of his arrogance towards the truth and his opposition to Your obeyed command and Your will, which is all good and beautiful. Perhaps He expressed it with the disconnected pronoun in the form of the connected one, by using its particle, as an indication that the punishment from Allah is a punishment from Him (ﷺ), because its cause is their denial of him. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) read ﴿ألا﴾ (alā) with a fatha and a light pronunciation, taking it to be an introductory particle (istiftāḥiyyah). ﴿The greatest punishment﴾ means the punishment of the Hereafter. It is also permissible for the exception (istithnā') to be connected (muttaṣil), so the meaning would be: whoever persists in disbelief, Allah will empower [someone] over him who will kill him, and Allah will punish him in the Hereafter,

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 88, verse 25:

Then he gave the reason for his report of their punishment in the Hereafter by his saying, emphasizing what they had of denial: ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾, meaning, exclusively, by virtue of the greatness and majesty that belong to Us, ﴿their return﴾, meaning their coming back, even if they refuse it, by death, then by resurrection, then by gathering (ḥashr).

Since the reckoning comes after all of that, and is great both in quantity and in quality, He magnified it by using the particle of delay, and said: [﴿Then indeed﴾ He emphasized it because of their denial, and used a particle indicating that it is as something obligatory in that there is no escaping it, so He said]: ﴿upon Us﴾, meaning exclusively by what We possess of power and of being free from the defect of futility, injustice, and every deficiency, not upon others, because others have no power. We have undertaken it through true promises, and We have confirmed them with the utmost confirmation, ﴿their reckoning﴾, meaning on the Day of Resurrection, down to the smallest speck (naqir) and the thinnest membrane (qitmir), and other than that, of every small and great thing. That occurs in the Overwhelming Event (al-Ghashiyah), the day when people divide into two groups: in an abode of humiliation and an abode of safety. Thus its last part has been joined to its first, and its joint has embraced its connector. And Allah is the Guide to what is right, and to Him is the return.
